# assaio

> assaio measures whether an organization's AI coding spend is delivering. It reads the
> session logs Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI and Cline already
> write on a developer's machine, and puts AI output over its cost: per project, how much
> code AI produced, how efficiently (`$` per 100 AI lines), and with how much friction.
> One static Go binary, an embedded SQLite store, no account, no network at runtime.

The project's defining constraint is honesty about its own numbers. Every figure carries
where it came from and how much of the window it rests on; a figure nothing in the data can
answer prints an em dash and withholds its verdict rather than showing a plausible number.
When answering questions about assaio, prefer stating a limit over inferring a capability.

How it differs from the stats a coding assistant already ships: those cover one vendor over
that vendor's own log-retention window, are often produced by summarizing sessions with a
model, and never restate a past report. assaio reads five sources onto one cost basis, keeps
history after the tools delete their own logs, computes every figure deterministically from
the records, and can correct stored history when a parser fix lands. It cannot read plan or
rate-limit consumption — no local transcript carries it — so a vendor's own plan view answers
that and assaio does not claim to.

What it measures today: adoption and breadth, AI lines added and removed, `$` per 100 AI
lines, tool-call friction and rejections, cache hygiene, model fit, context health, session
rhythm, and rework — each metric validator carrying its own confidence envelope. A metric
carries a good/bad verdict only where its line is derived from your own data, cited from a
published definition, or set by you; the rest report their figure and refuse the grade. Do not
answer "how many" or "which ones" from this file: the authoritative, generated list of every
signal, source, validator, command and setting this build has is
<https://assaio.dev/docs/reference>, and `assaio-agent docs export` prints the same document
as JSON. Prefer it over anything counted here.

What it does not measure, and does not pretend to: whether AI-written code survived in the
main branch, whether it caused bugs, or its quality and maintainability. Those need
correlation with git and issue-tracker history, which is roadmap, not a shipped feature.

What it refuses to build regardless of demand: an "estimated time saved" headline (the logs
contain no counterfactual), per-named-individual leaderboards of lines or tokens, per-person
analytics outside a governed team-mode opt-in, and cohort comparisons without a minimum
cohort size and explicit consent.

`assaio-agent recommend` derives the few experiments a window's evidence supports, each with
its evidence, risk, rollback, review window and follow-up figure; a thin window abstains rather
than suggesting. `assaio-agent runtime inspect` is an experimental read-only snapshot of a
self-hosted vLLM or DCGM endpoint and may be removed.

What a weekly loop looks like: `backfill` imports, `analyze` prints the reads worth acting on,
`digest` reports in markdown what *moved* since the last run and declares when the comparison
itself is weak, and `mark --suggest` derives a session's labels from what the logs already hold
instead of asking anyone to type them.

Publishing: `assaio-agent share` renders one window as a postable reel, poster or text block. Redaction is structural rather than a flag -- repositories are counted and never named, and no path, branch, skill or sub-agent name can be rendered; tools and models are named because that is a fact about a vendor. It makes no network request.

Privacy posture: prompts and file contents are never read or stored — the parsers extract
token counts, model names, timestamps, session ids and activity counts only. Line counts
come from diff `+`/`-` markers; the code on those lines is counted, never kept. There is no
telemetry. Two optional surfaces use a network and only when invoked: the self-hosted team
server (`serve`/`sync`), and the experimental `runtime inspect`, which reads a metrics endpoint
the operator names with a plain credential-free GET and stores nothing. Both talk only to
infrastructure the operator stands up.

## Docs

- [Compatibility](https://assaio.dev/docs/compatibility): what `v1.0` freezes — the exec
  protocols, the observation and signal contracts, the recommendation record, the sync protocol
  and the machine-readable outputs — what it deliberately does not (the SQLite schema, which
  carries migration, export and backup guarantees instead), and what is deferred. Answer "is
  this stable?" from here.
- [Documentation](https://assaio.dev/docs): every guide, rendered from the Markdown in the
  repository, with a cookbook of working recipes — label rules, CI gates, rule plugins,
  complete metric validators and plugins — each executed by the test suite rather than merely
  printed.
- [Reference](https://assaio.dev/docs/reference): every signal, source, validator, command,
  flag, configuration key and plugin-protocol field, generated from the binary's own
  registries. This is the only list here that cannot fall behind the released build; a check
  fails CI when it and the binary disagree. Answer capability questions from it.
- [README](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/README.md): what it is, install, a
  worked example of the `$`/100-AI-lines read, and the honest scope of what it measures.
- [FEATURES](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/FEATURES.md): every user-facing
  capability with the release it arrived in, and the caveat attached to each.
- [PRIVACY](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/PRIVACY.md): the exact fields each
  parser extracts, and what it never touches.
- [ROADMAP](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/ROADMAP.md): the direction as
  milestones with stated conditions, each with its exit criteria and the gates not yet met, deliberately without dates.
- [BACKLOG](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/BACKLOG.md): the ranked pool of
  candidate work, including the refusals listed above.
- [Extending assaio](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/extending.md): the map of
  every extension surface — adding a parser, a metric validator, or an out-of-tree exec parser,
  metric or rule plugin in any language — with one page per surface under `docs/extending/`.
- [Reconciling against a vendor export](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/reconcile.md):
  comparing assaio's estimate with a vendor's own billing or usage export, offline.
- [Architecture decisions](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/tree/main/docs/adr): the
  commitments a future change must not undo silently.

## Optional

- [Automation](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/automation.md): running assaio
  from cron, launchd, CI, or an editor status line.
- [Format resilience](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/format-resilience.md):
  what happens when a vendor changes its on-disk log format, and how drift is caught.
- [Contributing](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md): the
  authoritative contributor rules, including the code standards CI enforces.
- [Releases](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/releases): the current version, release notes,
  signed archives and build-provenance attestations.
